title: Sreeshankar Targets Glasgow Gold After Defying Career-Ending Knee Injury
excerpt: India's top long jumper heads to the Commonwealth Games as the season's Asian leader, two years after doctors told him he would never jump again.
body:
• Murali Sreeshankar, 27, heads to Glasgow as Asia's leading long jumper in 2026, with a season-best 8.38m that ranks eighth in the world.
  • The Kerala athlete targets a gold medal upgrade after winning silver at the 2022 Birmingham Commonwealth Games.
  • Sreeshankar's season marks a remarkable comeback from a ruptured patellar tendon in April 2024 that forced him to miss the Paris Olympics and prompted doctors to declare his career over.
  • India fields four long jumpers who have crossed 8.20m this season, signaling unprecedented depth in the event.

India's Golden Prospect

Murali Sreeshankar arrives at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow on July 23 as Asia's leading long jumper, carrying an 8.38m season best and the hard-won confidence of a man who was told two years ago that he would never jump again.

https://x.com/RevSportzGlobal/status/2079588313762255222

The 27-year-old from Palakkad, Kerala, produced that mark — his best since a personal-best 8.41m in 2023 — at the National Inter-State Championships in Bhubaneswar on June 28, where he recorded five jumps beyond eight metres en route to gold and earned the Male Athlete of the Meet award, according to myKhel. The performance currently ranks him eighth in the world for 2026.

"CWG and Asiad are always about the medal. Distance doesn't matter," Sreeshankar told The Times of India. "For both the competitions, 8.30-plus should be a medal-winning distance. Also, an 8.50m jump is very achievable for me if I keep following the same fitness, discipline and training drill."

"I can say that I'm probably in the best shape of my life. Just working on technical bits. If everything clicks, I'll jump well."

— Murali Sreeshankar, to The Times of India

A Comeback That Defied the Odds

Sreeshankar's presence on the start list in Glasgow would have seemed unlikely just over two years ago. In April 2024, a ruptured patellar tendon in his take-off leg — an injury virtually no long jumper had returned from at the elite level — ended his Paris Olympics campaign despite having already qualified.

The recovery involved open surgery in Doha, tendon reconstruction, hamstring grafting, and multiple anchor screws, according to myKhel. Several doctors in India told him his career was finished.

"I was told very frankly that I won't be able to jump again. Literally, I was told that my career was over," Sreeshankar recalled in an interview with The Times of India. "The path ahead was very unclear. There was very little literature on this injury and no standard recovery protocol."

He sat out all of 2024 and the first half of 2025, returning to competition before gradually rebuilding his form. A key turning point came when he qualified for the World Athletics Championships in Tokyo on the strength of his world rankings, according to Circle of Sport.

The Team Behind the Recovery

Sreeshankar credits physiotherapist Dr Priyam and strength and conditioning coach Dr Wayne Lombard with orchestrating his return. His father and longtime coach S. Murali — a former South Asian Games silver medallist in triple jump — remained a constant presence throughout.

"He is the Pied Piper who turns things around for me," Sreeshankar said of Lombard, speaking to myKhel.

The Athletics Federation of India and the Target Olympic Podium Scheme continued backing him even when a comeback appeared unlikely. "They trusted me more than I trusted myself," Sreeshankar said.

"Life teaches you a lot of lessons. I never expected that I will come back and jump this far consistently, when I first broke my knee."

— Murali Sreeshankar, to PTI

India's Long Jump Revolution

Sreeshankar is no longer a lone contender. India now boasts four jumpers who have crossed 8.20 metres in 2026 — Sreeshankar, Shahnavaz Khan, Lokesh, and David Patturaj Solomon — a depth that has transformed the domestic competitive landscape.

"8.20m is the new eight metres," Sreeshankar told myKhel. "I think India is the first country to have four jumpers above 8.20 metres. That's a remarkable feat."

Khan, who trains alongside Sreeshankar, produced a personal best of 8.30m at the same Bhubaneswar meet, qualifying for the Asian Games alongside his senior training partner, according to myKhel.

What to Watch in Glasgow

The men's long jump at Glasgow will test whether Sreeshankar can convert his Birmingham 2022 silver into gold. His 8.38m mark is within three centimetres of his lifetime best, and he has crossed eight metres in every outing this season — five competitions running.

After Glasgow, Sreeshankar plans Diamond League appearances in Monaco, Lausanne, and Zurich, followed by the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya in September, where he aims to upgrade the silver he won at the 2023 Hangzhou Games.

"I just want to upgrade my silver," he told myKhel. His operated knee is still not at 100 per cent, according to PTI, and each jump carries added weight. But for a man who rebuilt his career from a hospital bed, the stakes feel different now.

"I am always grateful for whatever I am doing. I am not taking anything for granted," he said.
